title: Python reset — CLI Expense Tracker
prerequisite: none assumed; verify your current Python level.
topics: Install/verify Python and run scripts from the terminal.
Variables, assignment, basic data types, type conversion.
Operators, expressions, comparisons, Boolean logic.
Input/output, formatted strings, basic validation.
Conditional statements and loops.
Lists, dictionaries, tuples, sets, indexing and iteration.
Functions, parameters, return values, scope.
Exceptions and basic error handling.
Read/write JSON; distinguish data from its file representation.
Import modules, use the standard library, organize a small project.
Git basics, repository initialization, commits, README, src/, tests/.
practice: Build a calculator, a list-based expense total, a dictionary representing one expense, and a JSON save/load exercise.
acceptance: Add, delete, categorize, list, and total expenses through a CLI; preserve data after restarting; handle invalid input; commit the project to GitHub with a README and basic tests.

title: Professional Python — Expense Tracker v2
prerequisite: Week 1 Python fundamentals and working CLI.
topics: File and package organization; imports and module responsibilities.
Iteration patterns, comprehensions, and appropriate data structures.
Function decomposition and separation of concerns.
datetime and date parsing/ranges.
CSV reading/writing and export formats.
Exceptions, validation, and meaningful error messages.
Configuration, paths, and safe file handling.
Unit tests, assertions, test cases, and edge cases.
Debugging with tracebacks and a debugger.
Virtual environments, pip, and dependency management.
Basic type hints, docstrings, and readable naming.
practice: Add CSV export, date filtering, category filtering, and tests for empty data, invalid dates, and missing files.
acceptance: Expense Tracker v2 supports filtering and export, passes automated tests, and has a reproducible setup documented in its README.

title: Git + HTTP + APIs — API Data Collector
prerequisite: Python functions, JSON, exceptions, and modules.
topics: Git staging, commit history, branches, merge conflicts, .gitignore.
GitHub repositories, pushes, pull workflow, and commit hygiene.
Client/server architecture, requests and responses.
HTTP methods, status codes, headers, query parameters.
REST API conventions and JSON payloads.
Use an HTTP client library such as requests or httpx.
Parse API responses and validate expected fields/types.
Timeouts, network failures, rate limits, and safe retries.
Environment variables and basic API-key handling.
Idempotency basics and logging failed requests.
practice: Call a public API, inspect the response, validate fields, transform the data, and save it as JSON.
acceptance: A repeatable API collector handles invalid responses and network errors, saves valid transformed data, and includes setup and usage documentation.

title: SQL + PostgreSQL — Database-backed application
prerequisite: data structures, JSON, HTTP responses, and basic relational concepts.
topics: Relational databases, tables, rows, columns, and schemas.
Data types, primary keys, foreign keys, and constraints.
SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE.
WHERE, ORDER BY, LIMIT, aggregates, and GROUP BY.
Joins and relationships between tables.
Normalization fundamentals and schema design.
PostgreSQL installation/setup and connecting from Python.
Parameterized queries and SQL injection prevention.
Transactions, commit/rollback, and basic integrity.
Index fundamentals and database error handling.
practice: Design a schema for customers, tickets, and ticket categories; query, insert, update, and delete records.
acceptance: Python fetches data from an API, validates it, and persists it in PostgreSQL using a sensible schema and parameterized SQL.

title: FastAPI — Customer Ticket API
topics: API routing, path/query parameters, request bodies.
Pydantic models, validation, serialization.
CRUD endpoints and appropriate HTTP status codes.
Dependency injection fundamentals.
PostgreSQL integration and database session lifecycle.
Configuration and environment variables.
API documentation and interactive OpenAPI docs.
Consistent error responses and endpoint testing.
practice: Implement a single ticket endpoint first, then add the remaining CRUD operations.
acceptance: A functioning ticket API supports POST/GET/PATCH/DELETE, validates requests, stores data in PostgreSQL, and exposes usable API documentation.

title: Backend completion — Portfolio Project 1
topics: HTTP and database integration tests.
Test fixtures and isolated test data.
Layered organization: routes, schemas, business logic, database access.
Pagination, filtering, and sensible validation boundaries.
Database migrations and schema change management.
Logging, exception handling, and configuration.
Git branches, clean commits, and issue-driven changes.
Architecture diagrams, screenshots, README, limitations.
practice: Write tests for nonexistent tickets, invalid payloads, duplicate or conflicting data, and database failures.
acceptance: A polished Support Ticket Backend repository with tests, architecture diagram, screenshots, setup instructions, and an explanation of the design.

title: LLM fundamentals — Python LLM CLI
topics: What LLMs can and cannot reliably do.
Model/API request-response flow.
System and user instructions; prompt structure.
Tokens, context windows, latency, and cost.
Temperature and generation settings at a conceptual level.
Nondeterminism and hallucinations.
Structured task definition and output requirements.
Basic output validation and failure handling.
Privacy considerations when sending customer data to external models.
practice: Classify a sample support complaint and request a category, priority, summary, and recommended action.
acceptance: A Python CLI takes a complaint and returns validated structured JSON, with sensible handling of malformed or incomplete outputs.

title: LLM APIs properly — Ticket Intelligence API
topics: API client setup, authentication, and model selection.
Structured outputs and schema validation.
Async requests when useful; request timeouts.
Rate limits, retries, error classes, and fallback behavior.
Token usage, cost tracking, and latency measurement.
Prompt versioning and repeatable test inputs.
LLM integration inside FastAPI.
Persisting model outputs and status in PostgreSQL.
Separating deterministic business rules from model decisions.
practice: Extend the ticket API to classify complaints, store the results, and expose an endpoint for classification.
acceptance: FastAPI → LLM → validated classification → PostgreSQL works end-to-end and can be tested without manually inspecting every response.

title: Embeddings + RAG concepts
topics: Embeddings and semantic similarity.
Vector representations and distance/similarity measures.
Retrieval-Augmented Generation: retrieve before generating.
Document ingestion, text extraction, and metadata.
Chunking, chunk size, and overlap.
Similarity search and top-k retrieval.
Grounded answers, source attribution, and abstention.
Basic retrieval-versus-generation failure analysis.
practice: Create a tiny document search over 10–20 documents and compare retrieved results with keyword search.
acceptance: A working document-search prototype can retrieve relevant passages and show where each passage came from.

title: PostgreSQL + vector search
topics: pgvector fundamentals and vector column storage.
Document/chunk/embedding data models.
Embedding generation and storage.
Similarity queries and top-k results.
Metadata filtering and document identity.
Re-ingestion, duplicate prevention, and update handling.
Connecting retrieval to a Python service.
Basic retrieval quality checks.
practice: Ingest documents, chunk them, generate embeddings, store them in PostgreSQL/pgvector, and retrieve relevant chunks.
acceptance: The retrieval pipeline is repeatable, persists vectors, returns relevant passages with metadata, and avoids accidental duplicate ingestion.

title: RAG chatbot — Portfolio Project 2
topics: Retrieval and generation pipeline design.
Prompting with retrieved context.
Citation IDs and mapping answers to source passages.
Refusing or abstaining when evidence is insufficient.
Handling irrelevant, conflicting, or incomplete context.
API integration and persistent document storage.
Separating ingestion, retrieval, and answer generation.
Manual testing of grounded and ungrounded questions.
practice: Test questions whose answers are present, absent, or ambiguous in the documents.
acceptance: A Company Knowledge Assistant provides source-backed answers and can decline to answer when the documents do not support a reliable response.

title: RAG quality — Evaluation dataset
topics: Build a representative dataset of 50–100 test questions.
Expected answers, evidence passages, and expected abstentions.
Retrieval relevance and recall concepts.
Answer correctness, faithfulness, and citation checks.
Repeatable evaluation runs and recorded results.
Failure categorization and error analysis.
Compare changes against a baseline.
Document limitations and known failure patterns.
practice: Run the same questions against two retrieval or prompting configurations and record which errors change.
acceptance: A repeatable evaluation report includes test inputs, expected outcomes, actual results, failure categories, and limitations.

title: n8n — First business workflow
topics: Workflow triggers and node-based execution.
Form submissions, webhooks, and payload structure.
Expressions, mapping, and conditional branches.
HTTP Request node and API authentication.
Connecting an LLM to a workflow.
PostgreSQL integration and notification delivery.
Execution history, retries, and error workflows.
Testing each node and the complete workflow.
practice: Build form → n8n → LLM classification → PostgreSQL → notification.
acceptance: A submitted form reliably enters the workflow, is classified, stored, and routed to the appropriate notification destination.

title: Business workflow automation — Lead Qualification
topics: Map a real business process from trigger to outcome.
Define qualification rules and required data.
Combine deterministic rules with AI classification.
Integrate CRM or a mock lead database.
Handle incomplete inputs and duplicate submissions.
Route leads by priority and qualification outcome.
Capture logs, workflow status, and failures.
Document the business problem and expected value.
practice: Build an automated lead intake and qualification workflow.
acceptance: The workflow routes sample leads consistently, records decisions, handles failures, and can be demonstrated as an agency-style project.

title: Tool calling — AI Support Agent v1
topics: Tool/function schemas and argument validation.
Model-selected actions versus application-executed actions.
Tool dispatch, results, and follow-up model calls.
Search-ticket and retrieve-knowledge tools.
Business rules, permissions, and tool boundaries.
Invalid arguments, tool errors, and execution limits.
Conversation state and traceable action records.
Testing correct, incorrect, and unnecessary tool calls.
practice: Let the model choose between searching the knowledge base and retrieving a ticket, while Python validates and executes the selected tool.
acceptance: The agent can select supported tools, produce valid arguments, handle tool failures, and explain its actions through recorded results.

title: Human-in-the-loop — Controlled AI actions
topics: Confidence scores versus calibrated confidence.
Decision thresholds and uncertainty.
Escalation rules and fallback behavior.
Human approval and rejection flows.
Audit logs and decision traceability.
Separation of proposed actions from executed actions.
Permissions and safe handling of sensitive operations.
Testing borderline cases and failure scenarios.
practice: Require human approval before a high-impact support action; let low-risk, explicitly permitted actions follow a controlled path.
acceptance: The workflow knows when to escalate, prevents unauthorized actions, records approval decisions, and safely handles rejected or timed-out approvals.

title: LangGraph — Controlled support workflow
topics: Graphs, nodes, edges, and conditional transitions.
State schemas and state updates.
Explicit workflow stages: classify → retrieve → decide → evaluate.
Tool integration within a graph.
Checkpointing and interruption concepts.
Human review and resuming workflows.
Loop prevention and termination conditions.
State-transition testing and trace inspection.
practice: Rebuild a limited support workflow as an explicit graph instead of adding another agent framework.
acceptance: A traceable workflow follows defined transitions, handles failures and approvals, and has tests for expected paths.

title: Testing AI systems — Automated evaluation harness
topics: Unit, integration, and end-to-end testing.
Deterministic mocks for external model APIs.
Dataset-driven evaluation of 100 questions.
Scoring functions and human-reviewed criteria.
Regression testing across prompt/model changes.
Tool-selection and argument-validity tests.
Latency, cost, failure rate, and outcome tracking.
Evaluation reports and reproducible runs.
practice: Run the agent against a fixed dataset, score its results, and produce a report identifying regressions.
acceptance: An automated test suite executes 100 questions, records scores and failures, and produces a report that another person can reproduce.

title: Docker — Reproducible environments
topics: Containers versus virtual machines.
Images, containers, Dockerfiles, and build contexts.
Ports, volumes, networks, and persistent database storage.
Environment configuration and secret handling.
Docker Compose services and dependencies.
Container logs, startup failures, and debugging.
Database readiness and health checks.
Reproducible local setup and clean shutdown.
practice: Containerize FastAPI, PostgreSQL, and the AI service with Compose.
acceptance: A clean environment can start the services using documented commands, persist database data as intended, and expose diagnosable logs.

title: Production architecture — Deployable AI workflow
topics: Structured logging and request/trace IDs.
Secret management and environment-specific configuration.
Timeouts, bounded retries, backoff, and idempotency.
Background jobs and long-running operations.
Database migrations and operational recovery.
Basic security, access control, and input validation.
Health checks, monitoring, and error reporting.
Cloud deployment, deployment configuration, and rollback concepts.
Deployment documentation and operational troubleshooting.
practice: Deploy a controlled AI workflow and test what happens when the model API, database, or downstream service fails.
acceptance: Another developer can deploy the system from the documentation, configure secrets safely, run tests, and diagnose common failures.

title: Capstone architecture — AI Customer Operations Platform
topics: Define the business problem, users, and success metrics.
Scope the minimum viable product and explicit exclusions.
Draw system architecture and data flow.
Design PostgreSQL schemas and vector storage.
Define API contracts and service boundaries.
Design document ingestion and RAG retrieval.
Design tools, n8n integration, and approval paths.
Define evaluation criteria and test data.
Break the implementation into testable milestones.
practice: Write a short technical specification before implementation.
acceptance: A scoped capstone specification connects each feature to a business need, test strategy, and measurable outcome.

title: Capstone reliability
topics: Input and output validation at system boundaries.
Edge cases, empty data, and malformed inputs.
Duplicate requests and idempotent operations.
Retry limits, timeouts, and recovery paths.
RAG grounding, citation correctness, and abstention.
Tool permissions, approval checks, and auditability.
Evaluation dataset of 100+ cases.
Documented scores, failures, and corrective changes.
practice: Build a failure-oriented test matrix covering API, retrieval, model, database, and workflow behavior.
acceptance: The platform has repeatable tests for reliability and AI quality, with 100+ evaluation cases and recorded results.

title: Capstone deployment
topics: Final Docker Compose configuration.
Deployment environment variables and secrets.
Database migrations and persistence checks.
Production-oriented README and architecture diagram.
API usage examples and setup instructions.
Health checks, logs, and known limitations.
Demo script and recorded demo video.
Fresh-environment deployment test.
practice: Have someone else follow your documentation or simulate a first-time user.
acceptance: The capstone is demonstrable, documented, deployable, and understandable without relying on undocumented steps.

title: Portfolio + CV
topics: Pin four repositories on GitHub.
Polish the three main projects and AI Evaluation Harness.
Use the Problem → Architecture → Implementation → Evaluation → Result → Limitations format.
Write project descriptions based on evidence.
Add diagrams, screenshots, setup instructions, and demos.
Describe your technical contribution accurately.
Rewrite CV bullets around demonstrated skills and outcomes.
Prepare concise project explanations.
practice: Explain each project in two minutes and then walk through its architecture.
acceptance: Your portfolio is coherent, reproducible, and supported by concrete evidence rather than unverified skill claims.

title: Applications + networking
topics: Analyze real job descriptions and required skills.
Match roles to verified project evidence.
Tailor CVs and applications.
Track applications, follow-ups, and response rates.
Contact startups, SaaS firms, agencies, and consultancies.
Prepare outreach around a concrete business problem.
Define a small, achievable freelance service.
Practice explaining business value and technical trade-offs.
practice: Submit targeted applications and send relevant, personalized outreach.
acceptance: An active application tracker, tailored materials, and a repeatable outreach process exist.

title: Interview + client readiness
topics: Explain Python, HTTP, SQL, APIs, and backend architecture.
Explain RAG, embeddings, evaluation, and model limitations.
Explain tool calling, approval boundaries, and reliability.
Debug a small unfamiliar problem under time constraints.
Discuss architecture alternatives and trade-offs.
Present project demos and evaluation evidence.
Answer behavioral and business-impact questions.
Continue applications and refine based on actual feedback.
practice: Run mock interviews, code reviews, and a simulated client discovery call.
acceptance: You can independently demonstrate your projects, explain important decisions, discuss limitations honestly, and respond to technical and business questions.
